01 — Why it matters

Manual THT insertion is the last bottleneck of the EMS line

SMT placement was automated decades ago. Through-hole is still done by hand — and the bench sets the pace of the whole factory.

01

The bench cannot be scheduled

A dozen or twenty operators, each inserting at their own rhythm. Output follows the shift roster, not the plan — and it drops when hands drop.

02

Wrong parts walk out the door

A reversed optocoupler, a connector with one un-bent lead, a relay that pops out in the wave — visual inspection catches some of it. The field catches the rest.

03

Odd-form means no standard answer

Tabs in reels, connectors in bulk, ICs in tubes, capacitors in trays — every packaging family needs its own feeding logic, so "just automate it" never fits one generic machine.

01

Load and index

The loader feeds panels onto the rail. Each machine clamps the board and indexes it under its heads — a 3-second board exchange between machines.

02

Feed per family

Vibration bowls for connectors and buzzers, tube feeders for optocouplers and eight-pin ICs, reel feeders for 187/250 tabs — every head gets the feeder its component family needs.

03

Insert at 0.4–0.8 s

Servo axes place and push each component; vacuum locates the body, the clamp holds it, the push rod drives it, and V-grooves guide the leads into the holes. Insertion direction is programmable 0–360° in 1° steps.

04

Clinch as you insert

The base die rises synchronously with the insertion and bends the leads while a circuit check confirms the part is seated — outward, inner, circular or two-turn bends per process requirement.

05

Detect before you place

Bowl optics reject wrong orientation and lead-deformed parts before the head picks them — no wrong parts, no wrong polarity reaching the board.

06

Wave solder downstream

Clinched boards ride the existing wave with leads already bent and held — the linkage prevents earlier-inserted components from popping out as later machines work the same panel.

Why the head and the base both move by servo

Servo head, servo base

The head structure and the base die are both servo-motor driven — the case document's own words: high stability, high speed.

Vacuum locate, cam clamp, push rod

Vacuum first positions the component by its body; the electric cam clamp grips the body shape and the push rod drives it down — the part is never held by its leads.

V-groove lead guidance

The gripper's V-groove devices align the lead tips before entry, so leads go into holes instead of onto pads.

Synchronous clinch die

As the component seats, the base die rises, a circuit check confirms it, and the leads bend in the same motion — outward, inner, circular or two-turn.

Built for linkage

Clinching during insertion is what lets five machines work the same panel in sequence without earlier components popping out.

Named-brand internals

THK ball screws (0.01 mm class), Panasonic AC servos, Airtac cylinders, SMC valves — serviceable anywhere, not just here.

Programming a process engineer can own

Online vision programming

Teach pick positions and mark points through the camera; vision correction compensates board placement.

Excel-like process editor

The case document describes the programming as a simple spreadsheet-style process — not a robot-language course.

USB import & serial link

Programs come in through USB or manual entry; RS-232C for the line handshake.

Orientation & lead checks

Bowl inspection checks part direction; the clinch die checks leads — rejects never reach the board.

10 — Insights

Eight short reads on automating the last manual bench

Everything we have learned putting odd-form insertion onto EMS floors. Full articles in English; summaries follow in your language.

ARTICLE 01The last manual bottleneck on your EMS floor

SMT ran at machine pace for decades. Through-hole still runs at hand pace — and everyone schedules around it.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Walk an EMS line from the solder paste printer to the wave and watch where the boards stop. They stop at the insertion bench. Placement is measured in CPH, reflow in profiles per hour — but the connector, the relay, the optocoupler and the big capacitor go in by hand, one pin-pair at a time, at the pace of whoever is on shift.

The cost is not only wages, and anyone who says "it's cheap labour" has priced only the visible line. The real cost is coupling: the bench sets the takt, so the wave solder runs when the bench feeds it, the testers idle when the bench falls behind, and every schedule promise your sales team makes is actually a promise about fourteen people's hands.

The second hidden cost is variance. A hand inserts a connector straight ninety-nine times and cross-threaded the hundredth. A missed clinch survives the bench and dies in the wave — the component floats up in the solder and the board comes back as scrap with a story about "quality problems." The insertion bench is where silent defects are born because it is the only station nobody instruments.

Here is what changed in the case behind this page: a power-board EMS factory put five linked odd-form insertion machines where the bench had been. Each machine took four or five component families, inserted at 0.4–0.8 seconds a part, bent the leads as it inserted, and passed the board downstream in three seconds. The bench did not disappear — it moved to machine tending, where one person covers two machines.

If you want the honest first step, do not buy anything yet. Time-study your insertion bench for one week: boards per shift, parts per board, minutes lost to rework, and every defect that traced back to insertion. Put the number on the wall. The wall is where the decision actually gets made.

ARTICLE 02Why odd-form components break standard insertion machines

Standard machines assume tape and reel. Your connectors assume bowls, tubes and trays — so automation has to start at the feeder.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Ask why axial and radial inserters have existed for fifty years while "odd-form" stayed manual, and the answer is one word: packaging. A resistor on tape is a solved problem — the machine knows exactly where the next part is, every time. A bulk 4-pin connector in a bag is four unsolved problems: orientation, singulation, presentation, and gripping a body that was never designed to be picked.

So the working method is not "buy a machine." It is a four-step ladder, and every successful odd-form cell we have built climbed it in the same order. Step one: sort by packaging family — reel tabs, tube ICs and optocouplers, bowl-fed connectors and buzzers, tray-loaded bulky caps. Step two: choose the feeder per family — reel feeders with cut-off for 187/250 tabs, tube racks for polarity-sensitive parts, vibration bowls with optical orientation check for bulk connectors. Step three: match the gripper to the body — vacuum plus a cam clamp that holds the component shape, never the leads. Step four: decide the lead treatment — which bends, which clinch die, how much holding force the wave will demand.

Factories skip steps and pay for it. The classic failure is buying the machine first and discovering the bowl feeder cannot present the connector without two pins bent — then the project dies in a pilot that "proves automation doesn't work here." The pilot did not prove that. It proved that step one was skipped.

The case line on this page ran the ladder properly: five machines, each with two to four heads, each head married to one feeder family — bowls for the yellow connectors, tubes for the optocouplers and eight-pin ICs, reels for the tabs, and clinch dies rising under every insertion. The result was 900 to 1,000 small boards per hour per machine, from the customer's own capacity table.

Send us your component list — the real one, with packaging as received — and we will sort it into the four families and tell you, part by part, which feeder answers it. That sheet is the beginning of every quote we make.

ARTICLE 030.4 seconds a connector: what a real insertion cell looks like

Inside the cycle: vacuum locate, cam clamp, V-groove guide, servo push, die rise — five motions in less than a second.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Slow-motion is the best sales demo we have, because the insertion cycle only looks simple until you watch it. A head comes down onto a bulk-fed connector in under a second, and five separate engineering decisions execute in that second.

First: the part is located by its body, not its leads. Vacuum grabs the silhouette of the component; the electric cam clamp closes on the body shape; the push rod drives from above. The leads are never load-bearing in the pick — that is why a 0.1 mm lead-deformation tolerance is printed in the spec table, not "whatever walks in."

Second: the leads find the holes through V-groove guides on the gripper. The tips are aligned before entry, so the part descends into its holes instead of hunting for them. Third: the Z servo pushes with a controlled force — the catalogue family holds insertion force limits (≤29.4 N typical, ≤98 N on heavy models) so a connector seats without cracking the board behind it.

Fourth: the base die rises at the same moment. This is the part people miss. The die does not wait for the insertion to finish — it rises synchronously, the leads pass its bending pockets, and a circuit check confirms the part is seated before the die folds the leads. Outward, inner, circular or two-turn bends, per process requirement. Fifth: the head retracts and the next feeder cycle has already presented the next part, because the bowl, tube or reel never stopped indexing.

Stack those cycles and you get the customer's own numbers: four to five placements per machine in 2.0–2.6 seconds, a three-second board exchange, 900–1,000 small boards per hour per machine. Not because any single motion is fast — because none of them waits.

The video cards above show exactly this cycle on two different boards — a yellow power board with connectors, a white control board with capacitors. Watch the die, not the head. The head is theatre; the die is the engineering.

ARTICLE 04Clinch first: the quiet reliability upgrade before the wave

A bent lead costs nothing and saves the board that floats out of the solder wave.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Everyone watches the solder joint. Almost nobody watches the lead that holds the component in place until the joint exists — and that invisible millimetre is where multi-machine lines live or die.

Here is the physics your wave solder applies: a river of molten tin pushing upward against every through-hole lead on the underside of the board. A component that is merely "inserted" is a component being pushed out of the board by a hydraulic hand. One lead straight, one lead crooked, and the part floats. On a manual bench with one part per hand per moment, floating is rare. On a linked line where a panel visits five machines before the wave, every earlier insertion is exposed to every later board movement.

The case document states the fix plainly: the head inserts, the base die rises synchronously, a circuit check confirms the lead position, and the die bends the leads — locking the component before the board ever leaves the machine. The document gives the linkage reason too: when multiple machines run in series, the clinch prevents previously inserted components from being pushed out by subsequent insertion forces.

Four bend geometries cover most products — outward, inner, circular, and two-turn — and the choice is a process decision, not a machine limitation. Light connectors take a simple outward bend; parts with short leads or high vibration duty take the two-turn. The die set is custom per product family, which is exactly the kind of engineering that pays for itself in the boards you stop losing.

There is a second dividend: clinched boards survive load, unload, conveyor transfers and manual touches without shifting. Your post-wave defect list gets shorter for reasons nobody can point at — which is the signature of a process that finally holds its own components.

If your current line runs insertion and clinching as two separate steps — or clinching as "the operator bends them" — tell us the component mix. We will show you which bend each family needs and what one die does to your float rate.

ARTICLE 05Feeding is the product: bowls, tubes, reels and trays matched per family

The machine gets the credit. The feeder does the work — and the packaging decision upstream is where the money is.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Ask any engineer who has run an insertion cell for a year, and they will say the same unfashionable thing: most stoppages are feeding stoppages. The head is fine. The part never arrived in the right attitude at the right place at the right time.

So treat the feeder as the product decision, and the four families each have a documented answer. Bulk parts — connectors, pin headers, buzzers — go to vibration bowls with optical orientation inspection, which the case document credits with rejecting wrong-direction parts before the head ever picks. The bowl is custom to the part, and that custom tooling is also your polarity guarantee: a reversed optocoupler cannot physically leave a correctly built bowl.

Tube-packaged parts — optocouplers, relays, side-actuated switches, eight-pin ICs — ride tube feeders. Tubes arrive from the component vendor already oriented, which is why the case document lists packaging-cost saving and recyclable tubes as a feeding advantage: the supplier's packaging becomes your magazine. Reel parts — 187 and 250 tabs — run on dedicated reel feeders with built-in cut-off, compatible across tab families, presenting each part at the pitch the head expects. Tray parts — bulky or sensitive — load from tray magazines with the same indexing logic as an SMT tray feeder.

The commercial move hides one level upstream. When you and your component buyer decide packaging together — bulk versus tube versus taped, which span, which orientation — you are not choosing boxes. You are choosing feeders, and feeders choose your uptime. The case line's component list reads like a feeder catalogue: reels for tabs, bowls for six connector types, tubes for four IC-family parts, bulk bowls for safety capacitors — and every one of them was a packaging decision before it was a machine decision.

Send the BOM with the packaging column filled in — that is the column most BOMs omit — and we will return the feeder map with it.

ARTICLE 06Fourteen operators, one line: the arithmetic of THT automation

The decision is not "machines versus people." It is a spreadsheet — and the spreadsheet says the bench is the most expensive station you do not measure.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Open any insertion project the way a plant manager actually has to: with numbers that survive a finance review. Start with the bench. Say a mid-size EMS line inserts ten odd-form parts per board across two thousand boards a day. At eight manual seconds a part — pick, orient, place, bend, inspect — that is 2,000 × 10 × 8 = 160,000 seconds, forty-four operator-hours every single day, before anyone counts breaks, rework or the shortage when two people call in sick.

Now the machine side, using the case document's published capacity: each inserter handles four to five families at 900–1,000 small boards per hour. Five machines clear the day's entire insertion load in one shift with margin — and they hold the same rhythm at 4 p.m. as at 8 a.m., because servos do not get tired, and clinch dies do not get bored.

The honest comparison is not fourteen operators versus five machines; it is forty-four operator-hours versus one line that needs tenders, not inserters. Operators move to loading feeders, first-piece verification and the quality checks the bench never had time for. The headcount does not vanish — it upgrades, which is also the answer to the workforce problem every EMS floor now admits: the young generation is not coming to sit at an insertion bench.

Then the payback, computed the boring way. The calculator above runs your own numbers: boards, parts, seconds, wage, days, price. In the case configuration — two thousand boards, ten parts, eight seconds, ninety-five percent freed — the addressed bench labour alone is tens of thousands of dollars a year, and the machines do the work at a fixed cycle the plan can trust. Quality gains, schedule gains and the rework list that shrinks are upside the model does not count.

Run your real numbers through it this week. If the payback is longer than two years, we will tell you so in the reply — that conversation has saved more projects than any brochure.

ARTICLE 07From one bench to a linked line: the upgrade path that keeps paying

Nobody automates everything at once. The factories that win automate in an order that funds the next step.

Articles are marketing commentary.

The question we get most is not technical: "Where do we start?" The answer has a shape — four steps, each one paying for the next, taken from how the best EMS floors actually rolled out THT automation.

Step one: the worst family. Pick the component family that causes the most insertion pain — usually the bulk connector that gets reversed, or the tab that gets missed — and put one machine with one bowl or reel feeder on it. One bench gone, one defect class gone, one internal team trained on vision programming. This step takes weeks, not quarters.

Step two: the second family, then the cell. A second machine doubles coverage and reveals the real lesson: changeover and feeding discipline matter more than headline speed. This is where the custom die sets and feeder library start accumulating — the asset that makes your next quote faster.

Step three: linkage. The case line shows the end-state: loader, five machines on conveyors, existing wave solder, unloader — 14,750 mm of documented line. Boards now move at a fixed three-second exchange, and the clinch-every-insertion rule is what makes the linkage possible at all. This is the step where takt becomes a number you publish instead of a hope you track.

Step four: the loop that keeps paying. New products come with new components, and every family you add reuses the feeder library, the die tooling and the programming skills you already built — the marginal automation gets cheaper than the first one. That is the compounding the bench never had: hands cost the same forever; a feeder library appreciates.

Keep the ladder visible on the wall next to the takt board. Teams that can see step three from step one do not abandon step two.

Already on step one? Send us the family that hurt most, and we will start the feeder map today — info@smthelp.com.

ARTICLE 08Send us your board file: the five-question insertion readiness check

Five questions separate a line that will run from a pilot that will stall. Answer them before you request a quote.

Articles are marketing commentary.

Every stalled automation project we have been called to rescue stalled on the same five questions. Answer them on paper before the machine conversation starts — including the ones where the honest answer is "we don't yet."

One: what exactly gets inserted? Not "connectors" — the list: every odd-form part, its packaging as received, its lead count and deformation tolerance. The case document's capacity table is built part by part; that granularity is what makes the quote real. Two: what does your board allow? Conveyor edge at least 5 mm, insertion holes at least 0.5 mm, body-to-body clearance 2 mm, leads straight within 0.1 mm. These are the documented machine requirements — and the design rules your PCB should be checked against before layout freezes.

Three: what holds the parts before the wave? Decide the clinch style per family — outward, inner, circular, two-turn — and what happens to parts you cannot bend. Factories that skip this question discover it in the solder pot. Four: what feeds the machine? Each family gets its answer — bowl, tube, reel, tray — and the packaging decision upstream belongs to purchasing, not to the machine vendor. Bring purchasing into the meeting.

Five: who will run it after we leave? Vision programming, Excel-style process editing and USB program import are designed so your engineer owns the line — but only if you name that engineer during commissioning, not after. The factories with the best uptime all made the same boring decision: one person, trained on day one, accountable forever.

Send the board file, the BOM with packaging, and your answers — we will run the five questions against them and reply with the feeder map, the die proposal and the capacity table, the same way this case study was built. info@smthelp.com · WhatsApp +86 13602562576.

13 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this case raises

Which components can this line insert?
The case line handles 187/250 reel tabs, bulk connectors from 2 to 7 pins, VH and horizontal connectors, pin headers, tube-packaged optocouplers, eight-pin ICs and side-actuated switches, bulk buzzers and safety/high-voltage capacitors, and tube relays. New families are matched with feeders, not refused.
Can it handle my bulk-packaged connectors?
Yes — that is the vibration bowl's job. The bowl is custom to the part, orients every piece, and optical inspection rejects wrong-direction parts before the head picks them.
What does my board need to support auto-insertion?
Documented rules from the case: conveyor edge ≥ 5 mm, insertion holes ≥ 0.5 mm, leads straight within 0.1 mm, body-to-body clearance ≥ 2 mm, board 100×100 to 380×280 mm on the case platform. Our THT design guideline PDF covers the full set.
How fast is insertion, really?
0.4–0.8 s per component depending on the part, with a 3 s board exchange. The customer's own capacity table gives 900–1,000 small boards per hour per machine for this product.
What is clinching and why does it matter before wave solder?
The base die bends the leads as the component seats — outward, inner, circular or two-turn. Bent leads hold the part against the upward force of the solder wave and against later insertions on linked machines, so nothing floats or pops out.
How many machines do I need?
The case split fourteen-plus component types across five machines by feeder family. Send your BOM with packaging and volumes — the machine count falls out of the feeder map and your takt, not from a brochure.
What utilities does each machine need?
On the case platform: single-phase 220 VAC, 2 kVA, and 0.5–0.6 MPa dry air at 0.6 m³/min. The S7900 catalogue lists higher head-count models at 4.5–6.6 kW max draw — plan per model.
Do we need robot programmers to run it?
No. Programming is online vision teaching plus an Excel-style process editor with USB import — designed for a process engineer, and included in commissioning training on your own board files.
